Then he sources the ability, saying his Lord taught it, which removes any suggestion of a craft he owns. Only then does he say what he has left behind. Commentators read the sequence as deliberate. He establishes credit, assigns it correctly, and uses it, all before touching the dreams the men actually asked about.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when the message was mostly being refused and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was speaking to individuals rather than crowds. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that Joseph is addressing men of a religion not his own, in a place where he has no standing, and that he begins from something they can verify rather than from a demand that they believe him.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb from the root for provision, so even prison rations are described as given rather than issued. The grammar puts a keeper of the stores behind the man who carries the tray.
Not a personal belief but the inherited practice of a people, the whole shape of how a community worships and lives. Leaving one was leaving a society, which is what makes the statement costly.

The verb is the one used for deliberate instruction of a student. Joseph presents his ability as curriculum received rather than talent possessed, which is how the surah has described it from the start.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food in confinement was brought at set hours by whoever the keeper sent, and what arrived depended on the day, the season and who was paying. Prisoners marked time by meals because there was little else to mark it by. Joseph's offer therefore uses the one regular event in his hearers' lives, and it can be checked within hours, which is a great deal more than a dream reading can offer.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Joseph uses for the way of a people occurs twice in this speech, once for what he has abandoned and once for what he follows, and those are the only two occurrences in the surah. The Quran uses the term throughout for inherited communal practice, which is why it appears most often in arguments about ancestors.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models how a claim about God is made credible. Joseph does not begin with doctrine; he begins with something testable, attributes it away from himself, and only then names what he has left and what he holds. It also shows knowledge treated as trust rather than property. What he can do is described as taught to him, which makes his skill an argument for the teacher rather than for the student.

crossReferences.why: The teaching promised to him as a boy, now being spent in a prison rather than a court.
The rest of this speech, where the alternative he follows is finally named.
Abraham reasoning his way out of an inherited creed, the same move made a generation earlier.

studies.applyIt: The next time you want to say something true and difficult to someone, notice what you offer first. Most of us lead with the conclusion. Try leading with something small they can check, then say the rest. Joseph spends a whole ayah earning the right to be listened to before he uses it.

studies.title: Scattered Lords Or The One
studies.meaning: He names his inheritance, then puts a question instead of an assertion. Are lords in pieces better, or God, the One, the Utterly Dominant. The comparison is about coherence rather than number: many masters mean divided authority, competing claims, and a servant who can never be sure which one he has failed. Commentators note that he addresses his listeners as fellow inmates, which places the question between equals and makes it hard to hear as a lecture from above.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca's shrine held many deities with overlapping functions, and traders would call on whichever suited a journey or a season. A community being asked to abandon that arrangement heard this argument as its own. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that Joseph traces a line through three named ancestors, which is precisely the kind of claim an Arabian audience weighed carefully.

keyTerms.note: The exact argument his listeners would have used against him is here turned around. He appeals to ancestry too, but to a line chosen for what it believed rather than for who happened to precede him.

A participle for things dispersed and pulling in different directions. Applied to lords it makes the objection structural: what is divided cannot be relied on, whatever the individual pieces are like.
An intensive form from a root for subduing completely, so that nothing can resist. It occurs six times in the Quran and every one of them joins it to the name the One.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan setting out would settle its obligations with several powers at once: a household god, a tribal patron at the shrine, a shrine keeper who took a fee. Divided loyalty was expensive as well as confusing, and a poor man's share of it was heaviest. Joseph's question would have landed on people who had spent their own money on exactly this arrangement and knew what it cost them.
studies.didYouKnow: The name Joseph reaches for in prison, the Utterly Dominant, appears six times in the Quran and is never used alone; each time it is preceded by the name the One. The pairing is spread across six surahs, so a formula first heard here from a prisoner returns later in scenes of creation and of judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Oneness is argued here from the servant's side rather than from metaphysics. A single authority means a single account to render, one standard, and no possibility of being caught between rival demands, which is a specific relief for a person with no power. The passage also shows a prophet reasoning with people rather than announcing to them: the form is a question, and it leaves them to answer.

crossReferences.why: Completes the argument by showing what the scattered lords actually are: names with nothing under them.
Uses the same pair of names for the day everyone finally stands before a single authority.
Puts the identical contrast as a parable of a man serving several quarrelling masters.

studies.applyIt: Write down, honestly, the three things whose approval most shapes what you do in a week. Not what you believe, what actually moves you. Then read them back and notice how often they pull in different directions. That tension is the thing Joseph is naming, and seeing it written is most of the work.

studies.title: Only Names You Have Named
studies.meaning: The argument is linguistic rather than metaphysical. What his fellow prisoners serve, Joseph says, are names, invented by them and by their ancestors, with no warrant sent down for any of them. The objects exist; what does not exist is the authority the names claim. He then places judgement with God alone and calls this the upright way, adding that most people do not know it. Commentators read the last clause as descriptive, not dismissive.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The shrine at Mecca held images whose names had been in use for generations, and the standing of each was largely a matter of inherited custom rather than any claim to revelation. This ayah dismantles exactly that arrangement. No occasion is reported for it. The commentators observe that Joseph is making the argument to two prisoners, not to a court, which is where the surah keeps placing serious speech.

keyTerms.note: A noun followed by its own cognate verb, so the sentence circles back on itself. The construction traps the naming inside human authorship: the word came from you and points nowhere beyond you.

Not power in general but a sanction that entitles a claim, the way a written order entitles an official. The objection is that nobody can produce one, which makes the practice groundless rather than merely mistaken.
The adjective means standing straight and also self-sustaining, from the same root as one of the great divine names. A way of life described as upright is one that does not need propping up.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Naming was serious business in Arabia. A poet could fix a man's reputation with an epithet, tribes were known by names given to ancestors, and an idol's name carried the weight of everyone who had used it before you. To be told that a name is merely a name, invented and passed on, struck at how that society assigned value to almost everything, not only to its gods.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence placing judgement with God alone occurs three times in the Quran, and two of those are in this surah: here from Joseph in prison, and later from Jacob sending his sons to Egypt. The same words are spoken by a father and a son who at that point have not seen each other for many years.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Idolatry is diagnosed as a failure of evidence rather than of taste. The question the passage puts is simply where the authority came from, and it applies well beyond carved images to anything a person serves because it has always been served. Placing judgement with God alone also has a levelling effect: a prisoner and a governor are answerable in the same court, which is the point the speaker's own situation makes for him.

crossReferences.why: Jacob uses the identical sentence about judgement, in a very different kind of difficulty.
Repeats the charge that the objects of worship are names, invented and unsupported by anything sent down.
An earlier prophet makes the same argument to his people about names inherited from their ancestors.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you defer to without ever having asked why: a rule at work, an assumption about what a good life looks like, a piece of advice you repeat. Ask where the authority for it came from. Not to overthrow it. Most will survive the question, and the two or three that do not are worth finding.

studies.title: The Matter Is Settled
studies.meaning: He gives both readings plainly and does not cushion the second. One will pour wine for his master again; the other will be executed, and birds will feed from his head. Then a single clause closes the exchange: the matter you are asking about is decided. Commentators record a report that one of the two men then claimed he had invented his dream, and they read the final sentence as Joseph's reply. Once a thing is settled, retracting the question changes nothing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a community that could imagine execution for what it believed and had already seen its weakest members abused. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that Joseph delivers the harsher reading last and without hedging, which is how the surah presents prophetic speech generally: accurate, unwelcome where it must be, and not adjusted to the hearer's preference.

keyTerms.gloss: he will pour for his master
keyTerms.note: The word for master here is the ordinary one for a lord or owner, the same word used of God elsewhere. Its double life runs through this surah and is part of what makes some sentences in it read two ways.
A passive verb naming a specific public execution, with the body left exposed. The Quran uses it for a punishment inflicted by rulers, and the detail about birds belongs to that exposure.
A passive with no agent named, which is how the Quran often marks a settled decree. The same phrase appears in later surahs at the point where nothing further can be revised.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bodies were sometimes left where everyone could see them, and everyone understood why. Exposure denied a family the burial that closed a death, and carrion birds finished what the sun began. In Arabia this was the fate of the outcast and the enemy, and a listener needed no explanation of the image. The horror in the sentence is not the dying. It is what is refused afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause that closes this ayah, the matter is decided, recurs elsewhere in the Quran at moments when the time for changing anything has passed. It is spoken again in a later surah by the enemy of humanity himself, addressing his followers after judgement, which places the same three words in the mouths of a prophet and of a deceiver.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowing the future is shown to be a different thing from controlling it, which is the surah's steady position. Joseph is given an accurate reading and cannot alter what he reads. The passage also refuses the comfort of vagueness. A message that softens itself to spare the hearer is not a message, and the Quran's prophets are repeatedly shown declining that softening even when they are the ones who will pay for it.

crossReferences.why: The reading proves accurate, and the survivor's release is where the next turn begins.
The same phrase about a settled matter, spoken after judgement by the one who misled people.
Joseph names this prison years later as the place God brought him out of.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of news you have been softening for someone, or for yourself. You do not have to deliver it today. Write it once in the plainest sentence you can manage, with no cushioning clause before or after. Then decide separately whether and when to say it. The two decisions are not the same.

studies.title: Mention Me To Your Master
studies.meaning: One word does all the work in this ayah, and it turns twice. Joseph asks to be mentioned; then Satan makes someone forget the mention of his lord, and years pass. The pronouns are deliberately open. Scholars differ: many read the cupbearer as forgetting to speak of Joseph to the king, others read the forgetting as Joseph's own, a moment of leaning on a man instead of God. The Arabic supports both, and the classical commentaries record the range without insisting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was watching for a break in its situation and repeatedly finding that promised help from people did not arrive. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that the story has been running for roughly a decade at this point, and that the surah passes over those years in a single closing clause.

keyTerms.gloss: mention me, keep me in mind
keyTerms.note: The root covers speaking of something and holding it in mind at once, which is why the same word names the remembrance of God. Joseph's request and the failure that follows use one term.
A causative: someone was made to forget rather than simply forgetting. The subject and object are both left open by the grammar, which is where the difference among the classical readings begins.

The classical lexicons define this number word as somewhere between three and nine. The surah declines to be more exact, and the vagueness is the point: nobody in a cell counts a term that has no end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A word in the right ear was how anything got done. Petitions moved through servants, kinsmen and clients rather than through offices, and a released prisoner carrying a name to a ruler was the ordinary mechanism of appeal. Everyone listening had asked someone for exactly this favour, and most had waited for it. What the ayah describes is not betrayal. It is how quickly a promise dissolves once the person making it is comfortable again.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for several years appears only twice in the Quran: here, and at the opening of a later surah where it marks the term within which a defeated empire would win again. In both places it measures a wait whose length nobody is told, and both waits end exactly as promised.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Human help is not forbidden and it is not reliable, and the surah lets both facts stand. Joseph asks a man for something reasonable and receives nothing for years, and the story does not treat him as having sinned. What it does is attach the failure to forgetting, which the Quran consistently treats as the characteristic human fault, and which is answered throughout the Book by the discipline of remembrance.

crossReferences.why: The forgetting ends: the released man remembers, in the same root, after a long time.
Attaches a phrase of remembrance to the human tendency to forget, in almost these terms.
Names forgetting the remembrance of God as the work of the same enemy at issue here.

studies.applyIt: You are waiting on someone who said they would help. Send one short message this week, without reproach, and then set the matter down. Ask God for the same thing in the same hour. This ayah is not against asking people. It is about where the weight of your waiting is resting.

studies.title: Seven Fat And Seven Lean
studies.meaning: The dream is agricultural accounting rather than symbolism. Cattle and grain were the two things a Nile economy counted, and the vision gives each of them a run of seven and then a reversal, with the lean consuming the fat. The king reports it and asks his council for a reading, and his phrasing concedes something in advance: if you are able to interpret visions. A ruler who has to add that clause already suspects the answer he is going to get.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a city that lived on trade and on grain brought in from elsewhere, and which knew what a bad season did to prices. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators observe that the surah gives the ruler no name and no dynasty, calling him only the king, in contrast to the accounts of Moses where a title is used. The Quran keeps the focus on the office.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective for animals in good condition. In a herding economy the word is a measure of the year rather than of the beast, since cattle carry visible evidence of how the pasture has been.
An unusual plural for emaciation, used of animals whose flesh has gone. The pairing with the previous word is a stock contrast in Arabic, and the dream sets them eating each other, which is not.
The inner circle around a ruler, from a root about being filled. The Quran uses the word for the men who fill a court and whose agreement a ruler needs, and it is rarely complimentary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Egypt fed the region. Grain moved north and east along routes Arabian traders used, and a failure in the Nile flood raised the price of bread from Syria to Yemen. Mecca itself imported most of what it ate. A dream about seven bad harvests was not a curiosity to the surah's first hearers; it described the mechanism by which their own city could go hungry within a season.
studies.didYouKnow: The dream is repeated three ayat later almost word for word, when the released prisoner carries it to Joseph. Apart from the grammatical endings the two lists are identical, so the Quran transmits the vision twice without paraphrase, which is how an accurate report travelled in an oral culture and how the surah shows this one arriving intact.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provision is presented as something that moves in cycles a society can neither predict nor control, which is the plain economic fact the ayah begins from. The dream is given to the one person able to act on it, and he cannot read it. That mismatch, power without understanding, sets up the rest of the surah, where the reading turns out to be held by a foreigner in a cell.

crossReferences.why: The dream is repeated to Joseph in nearly identical words, which is how the reading is obtained.
The answer, which converts the images into a seven-year plan and adds a year nobody asked about.
Addresses fear of scarcity directly, and places the providing where this story places it.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you are living on now as though it came in seasons: a job, a body, an income, a run of good health. Write down what you would do differently if you knew this was a fat year. You do not have to act on it today. The question changes how the year feels while it lasts.

studies.title: Jumbled Dreams, They Said
studies.meaning: The council gives a diagnosis and then a confession, and the second half undoes the first. Jumbled dreams, they say, and then: we know nothing of interpreting dreams. If the second sentence is true the first was not a reading but a way of closing the subject. Into that gap steps a man who has been out of prison for years and remembers only now. The Arabic says he remembered after a long stretch, which is the surah's driest sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca's own leaders had a habit of dismissing what they could not answer, and the audience for this surah had heard the message called poetry, sorcery and confused dreaming in their own assemblies. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that the court's failure is honest as far as it goes, and that the fault lies in the confident label offered before the admission.

keyTerms.note: The first word means a handful of mixed stalks tied together. It turns the dream into a bundle of unrelated scraps, which is a way of saying that nothing in it needs explaining.
The negation is emphatic and the word is the ordinary one for those who know. They are not saying the dream is unreadable, only that nobody in the room can read it, which is a different admission.
A worn-down form of the verb to remember, and one of several places where Arabic smooths a difficult consonant cluster. It is the same root as the request Joseph made to him years earlier.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Courts everywhere kept men whose business was reading omens, and their standing depended on never being at a loss. Admitting ignorance in front of a ruler was dangerous, which is why the first answer arrives with a label attached. Arabian assemblies worked the same way. A man who could not answer changed the subject with a phrase, and everyone present understood the manoeuvre.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase the council uses for jumbled dreams occurs only twice in the Quran. The other place is a later surah where opponents of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) reach for the same words to dismiss the revelation itself. The identical formula is used once by a court that cannot read a dream and once by men who will not read a book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two things easily confused: not knowing, and covering the not knowing with a name. The Quran treats the first as ordinary and the second as the beginning of refusal. It also marks how understanding actually reaches a court, arriving not through its experts but through a servant's memory, which is one of the surah's repeated arrangements for how God moves things.

crossReferences.why: The same phrase used to dismiss the revelation, by men who then demand a sign instead.
The request this man forgot, made with the same verb he finally acts on here.
Sets the limit the council should have started from: you have been given only a little knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Try saying I do not know once today, out loud, in a setting where you would normally produce a name for the thing instead. Notice what happens next in the conversation. Very often the person who admits it is the one someone finally tells the truth to.

studies.title: Joseph, Man Of Truth
studies.meaning: The man arrives with a title, a question and no apology. He calls Joseph by an intensive form meaning utterly truthful, which is a considerable thing to say to a man his silence helped keep in prison. Then he asks for the reading and explains why: so that I may go back to the people and they may know. Commentators notice what is missing. He does not mention the promise he failed to keep, and he does not ask whether Joseph would like to leave.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community hearing this knew what it was to be sought out for something useful by people who had otherwise abandoned them. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note the courtesy of the address, which suggests the released man had told the court where the reading would come from, and that Joseph's reputation had survived a decade of confinement intact.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the word for truthful, meaning one whose truthfulness has become a settled character. The Quran applies it elsewhere to Abraham, to Idris and to Mary, so it is a considerable title.
A verb for seeking an authoritative opinion on something difficult. It concedes expertise to the person asked, which is why the king used it to his own council and got nothing back.
The particle carries hope rather than certainty. He wants to bring an answer back, and the phrasing admits that whether the court accepts it is not in his hands.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Titles did real work in that world. Calling a man truthful in public was a kind of surety, and the speaker's own standing was staked on it. Arabian society ran on such words: a man vouched for, a man whose word was accepted, a man nobody would trade with. Using this title inside a palace, about a prisoner, was a small act with a cost attached.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive form used here for one who is utterly truthful is applied in the Quran to a small handful of figures, including Abraham, Idris and Mary. In this surah it is not given to Joseph by God or by the narration, but by a man who had forgotten him for years, which makes it the verdict of someone with no reason to flatter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reputation is shown outliving circumstance. Nothing in Joseph's situation had improved and the description of him had not weakened, which the surah offers as evidence about character rather than about luck. The passage also shows how usefulness reopens doors that justice did not. He is fetched because the court needs something, and the Quran reports that without cynicism and without pretending otherwise.

crossReferences.why: The dream repeated here almost word for word, transmitted intact from the king to the cell.
The same title of utter truthfulness given to Abraham, which sets the weight of the word.
The public confirmation that this description of him was accurate all along.

studies.applyIt: Say the good thing about someone in the room where it costs you something, not in the room where it is easy. A word of vouching in front of people who can act on it is worth a year of private admiration. Pick one person this week and one room, and use their name.

studies.title: Leave It In The Ear
studies.meaning: The reading of the dream is not offered as a reading. Joseph moves straight to instructions, and they are technical: farm steadily for seven years, then leave what you harvest in its husk, eating only a little. Storing grain unthreshed keeps it from spoiling and from being eaten, which is practical knowledge rather than prophecy. Commentators note that he answers a question about symbols with a policy, and that the interpretation is left to be inferred from the plan.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Storage was the difference between a lean year and a famine, and every settlement the first hearers knew kept some kind of reserve. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators observe that Joseph gives the plan before any offer has been made to him, while he is still in prison and has been promised nothing, which is why they read the passage as advice given rather than a bargain struck.

keyTerms.note: Habitual persistence at hard work, from a root about keeping at something. The same root describes the sun and the moon in a later surah, ceaselessly running their courses.
The head of the grain stalk. Leaving the crop unthreshed was the standard way to protect it from damp and vermin, so the instruction is agricultural technique rather than a symbol.
The exception carved out of the whole harvest. It concedes that people must eat during the good years, and sets the bar for consumption at the smallest amount that lets them do so.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grain kept in the ear could sit for years in a dry store; threshed grain drew insects and rot within months. Farmers everywhere knew this, and communities that survived lean seasons were the ones with the discipline to leave full granaries alone while times were good. In Arabia the same principle governed dates and water. Nobody argued with the technique. What was hard was doing it seven years running.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for steady, unbroken effort in this ayah appears only once in the Quran in this form. Its root returns two surahs later, describing the sun and the moon as continuously pursuing their courses, so the same idea of tireless regularity is used once for how a nation should farm and once for how the heavens move.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Foresight given by God is handed over as a workable plan rather than kept as a marvel. The passage treats prudence as a form of gratitude: the good years are a gift, and the fitting response is restraint rather than consumption. It also sets an unusual bar. Seven years of eating less while the harvest is abundant asks more of a people than a single act of sacrifice would.

crossReferences.why: Completes the plan with the hard years and with a further year nobody had asked about.
Uses the same root for tireless continuation, of the sun and the moon in their courses.
Places the same restraint at the level of an individual meal rather than a national store.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you currently have more of than you need, this month specifically. Money, time, energy, food in the house. Set aside a small fixed part of it before the month starts rather than after it ends. The size matters far less than the order, which is the whole content of this ayah.

studies.title: Then A Year Of Relief
studies.meaning: Two ayat finish the plan and then add something nobody asked for. Seven hard years will eat the stores, except a little kept back; then a year comes in which people are given relief and press their harvest. The dream held fourteen images and Joseph reads a fifteenth year out of it, which the commentators discuss with interest. The verb for that relief is the same root as the word for rain, so the sentence promises water and rescue in one word.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Rain in Arabia was the difference between a year and a famine, and the vocabulary for it was correspondingly rich. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that Joseph offers the final year as part of the reading rather than as consolation, and several observe that he is describing the end of a hardship to a court that has not yet begun to feel its beginning.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective for years, from the root for tightness and strength. Arabic names a bad year by how it grips rather than by what it lacks, which is closer to how such a year is actually experienced.
From the root for a fortress. Grain held back is spoken of as garrisoned, which fits the surrounding language: a store is a defended place and consumption is the breach in the wall.
The root gives both the word for rain and the cry for help, so a single passive verb here means rescued and rained upon at once. English needs two words and loses the join.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A season without rain reorganised everything. Herds were sold cheap, then died; families moved towards wells and towards relatives with water; debts were taken on that outlasted the drought by a generation. When rain finally came the whole settlement went out to it. The Arabic word for that arrival is the same one used here, which is why the last clause would have felt to the first hearers like the door opening.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as being given relief comes from the root behind the ordinary Arabic word for rain, and behind the cry a person makes when calling for rescue. One consonantal root covers water falling, help arriving and a shout for aid, so the good year at the end of Joseph's reading is described in a word that already carries the sound of asking.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reading refuses to end at the bad part. Seven hard years are stated plainly and then placed inside a longer shape that includes their ending, which is how the Quran generally handles hardship: not denied, not minimised, and not treated as the last word. Naming rain as relief also puts the recovery outside human management. The stores are the work of the plan; the year that ends the famine is not.

crossReferences.why: The first half of the same plan, which the hard years here are designed to be met with.
Describes God sending rain after people have despaired, and calls Him the Protector.
Traces the same sequence from despair to rain to a dead land returned to life.

studies.applyIt: When you next describe a hard stretch to someone, add the sentence about afterwards. Not a promise about outcomes, only the honest observation that it will have an afterwards. Most of us narrate difficulty as though it were the shape of the whole thing. Joseph gives seven bad years a boundary in the same breath as he names them.

studies.title: Ask Him About The Women
studies.meaning: The door opens and he does not walk through it. The king sends for him and Joseph sends the messenger back with a question instead: ask about the women who cut their hands. He is not requesting release, and he is not accusing anyone. He is asking for the record to be examined before he leaves, so that whatever happens next rests on a finding rather than on a favour. The closing clause hands the knowledge of it all to God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a period when the community was occasionally offered relief on terms that would have left the accusations against it standing. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators dwell on the restraint of the request: Joseph names no one, brings no charge against the household that imprisoned him, and asks only that an existing episode be looked into by the authority that can look into it.

keyTerms.note: A plain imperative sent to a royal envoy. The bluntness is part of the scene: a prisoner declines a summons and returns the messenger, which is not how such invitations were usually answered.
A formula for asking after the state or condition of something. It opens an enquiry rather than making an allegation, which is exactly the difference Joseph is being careful about.
The surah's recurring word for covert contrivance, now placed under God's knowledge rather than a human court's. Joseph asks men to investigate and simultaneously says who already knows the answer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour, in that society, was not a feeling but a public status that determined whether people would deal with you, marry into your family or accept your testimony. A man released without a finding carried the charge with him for life, and his children carried it after him. Everyone hearing this understood that walking out of the prison quietly would have cost Joseph more than the years had.
studies.didYouKnow: Across the whole surah Joseph never once asks a human being to release him. He makes exactly one request of a person, when he asks a fellow prisoner to mention him to the king, and it goes unanswered for years. Here, offered his freedom outright, what he asks for instead is an investigation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being cleared and being released are treated as different goods, and the passage puts the first ahead of the second. That is a claim about what a person owes to the truth about themselves, and it holds even when the delay is costly. The final clause keeps it from becoming pride: the scheming is already fully known to God, so the enquiry is for the record among people rather than for the record that matters.

crossReferences.why: The enquiry is held, and the truth is stated publicly by the person who buried it.
The one request Joseph made of a human being, and the years of silence that followed it.
Another moment where he refuses the convenient outcome and insists on the correct one.

studies.applyIt: If there is a misunderstanding about you that you have been living with because clearing it up would be awkward, take the smallest possible step this week. One question to one person who was there. Not to win the argument, and not to make anyone apologise. Only so that the record is not left as it stands.

studies.title: Now The Truth Has Surfaced
studies.meaning: The enquiry is held and it produces two answers. The women say they knew no evil of him, which is careful and partial. Then the one person who could end it does: I tried to seduce him, and he is telling the truth. The verb she uses appears nowhere else in the Quran and means a buried thing has come up into view, the way grain separates from chaff. She says it without being pressed, in public, when nothing further depends on the lie.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. A public retraction in that society cost the speaker standing that could not be recovered, since honour was held collectively and a household bore the damage together. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators observe that the king's question is put to the women rather than to her, and that she volunteers her part of it, which is what turns an investigation into a confession.

keyTerms.note: A formula for asking about a serious matter, from a root connected to formal address. The king opens with the language of an enquiry rather than of an accusation, which leaves room for what follows.

Occurring only here in the Quran, the verb describes something buried working its way up into plain view. The lexicons connect it to grain separating from husk, so the truth is pictured as emerging rather than announced.
The word the brothers claimed for themselves under a conditional in the surah's first scene. Here it is finally awarded, in public, by the person who had the most to lose from awarding it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the machinery of justice, and testimony against your own interest carried enormous weight precisely because nobody gave it lightly. An Arabian audience knew the difference between a man cleared by his relatives and a man cleared by his accuser. The second could not be argued with. When she speaks, the case closes in a way no amount of advocacy on Joseph's behalf could have closed it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb she uses for the truth coming out occurs exactly once in the entire Quran, in this ayah. Arabic has many ordinary words for something becoming clear, and the Book reaches instead for one that appears nowhere else, at the moment a matter buried for more than a decade finally works its way to the surface.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repentance is presented here without any of its usual furniture. There is no plea, no promise and no request; there is a plain statement of what she did, made where it can be heard. The Quran treats that as the substantive part. The passage also shows truth being restored by the person who damaged it, which is the pattern the surah will repeat when the brothers speak at the end.

crossReferences.why: The private admission this makes public, spoken years earlier in a room full of guests.
The brothers make the same kind of unforced public admission at the surah's other reckoning.
Asks for testimony given for the sake of fairness even when it runs against the speaker.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small thing you let stand that is not quite true, about a colleague, a sibling, a version of events you never corrected. Correct one this week, in front of whoever heard the first version. Say what happened and stop. You will find the whole exchange takes about eleven seconds.

studies.title: I Did Not Betray Him Unseen
studies.meaning: Who is speaking here is one of the classical questions of the surah. Many commentators continue the woman's speech, so that she is saying she did not betray her husband while he was absent, having now told the whole truth. Others give the words to Joseph, reporting back on why he sent the messenger away: so the man would know that nothing was done behind his back. Both readings are old, both are defensible, and the ayah works either way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's audience lived where a household's reputation belonged to everyone in it, and where an absent man's affairs were held in trust by those who remained. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators discuss the ambiguity at length and largely decline to close it, which is itself a useful record of how the classical tradition handled a genuinely open sentence.

keyTerms.note: The word for what is hidden from view, used across the Quran for the realm beyond perception. Here it means simply behind someone's back, and the choice of term quietly links the two ideas.

The root is specifically about breaking faith with something entrusted to you, not about deception in general. It names a failure of custody, which is the relationship at issue in every version of this reading.
The verb usually takes a person as its object. Here it takes a scheme, so the sentence says that a plan built on breach of trust is not brought to its destination, whatever its author intends.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long absences were normal. A man went with a caravan for months, and everything he owned, including his household's good name, was left in the keeping of people who stayed. That arrangement only worked because breaking such a trust was among the most serious things a person could do. The Arabic word for it here is the word used of a man who takes a deposit and does not return it.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah has no explicit subject, and the classical commentaries divide over who is speaking, some continuing the previous speaker's words and others handing them to Joseph. Both readings were current among the earliest generations, and the major commentaries record the disagreement side by side rather than settling it, which is how the tradition handles a genuinely open pronoun.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah defines integrity by what happens when nobody is watching, and then gives the verdict on the alternative: schemes built on broken trust are not brought home. That is stated as a general law rather than as a wish, and the surah has been demonstrating it since the first scene. Every plan made in secret in this story has arrived somewhere other than where its author aimed.

crossReferences.why: The refusal this sentence looks back on, made behind closed doors with nobody watching.
Names betrayal of a trust as a distinct failure, separate from other kinds of wrongdoing.
Shows a plan reaching its intended end only because God willed it, not by its own cleverness.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing that is yours to look after and that nobody checks: a shared account, a set of keys, someone's private words, an hour you are paid for. Do that one thing carefully today, on purpose, while noticing that no one will know. That noticing is the exercise, not the care.

studies.title: Except Whom My Lord Has Mercy
studies.meaning: The sentence begins by refusing a claim: I do not declare myself innocent. Then comes the famous phrase, in an intensive form that describes a soul persistently urging towards harm rather than doing so once. The exception is the whole ayah. Only mercy interrupts the pattern, and the closing names God as Forgiving and Merciful rather than as strict. As with the previous ayah, commentators differ over the speaker, and the statement carries either way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah reached people who were being asked to hold a difficult line for years without visible reward, and who would have known exactly how unreliable their own resolve felt from the inside. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that whichever speaker is assigned to it, the sentence is spoken at a moment of vindication rather than of failure, which is what makes it striking.

keyTerms.note: A verb for clearing someone of a charge, from the root behind healing and being quit of a debt. Refusing to apply it to oneself is a legal image: I do not issue myself an acquittal.
An intensive pattern, the same shape as the divine name meaning the Utterly Dominant used earlier in this surah. It describes a settled habit of commanding, not a single impulse.
The verb behind the two great names in the opening formula of every surah. It is the only thing in the sentence that stands against the pattern just described, and it is placed as an exception.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A commander in that world was someone whose orders came without explanation and were obeyed before they were weighed. Households, caravans and war parties all worked this way, and the word used here for the soul is the word for that kind of authority. The image would have landed on people who knew what it was to find themselves already halfway through obeying something.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase describing a soul that persistently urges towards harm occurs once in the Quran, in this ayah. Later tradition took the phrase and set it alongside two other Quranic descriptions of the soul, one self-reproaching and one at peace, to build a threefold account that the Book itself never assembles in one place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Self-knowledge here is not despair. The ayah states the human condition accurately and then places mercy over it, in that order, which keeps honesty about oneself from collapsing into either excuse or hopelessness. It also removes any ground for looking down on others, since the description is offered in the first person by a speaker who has just been publicly cleared. Nobody in this surah is allowed to issue their own acquittal.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same pull checked from outside, by a proof shown rather than by resolve.
Names the self-reproaching soul, the second of the descriptions later tradition set beside this one.
Names the soul at peace, addressed and called back at the end of its testing.

studies.applyIt: The next time you avoid something wrong, try finishing the thought differently. Instead of noting that you are the kind of person who would not do that, say plainly that you were kept from it. It sounds like a small edit. Over a few weeks it changes how you look at people who did not manage it.

studies.title: Put Me Over The Storehouses
studies.meaning: The king offers closeness and Joseph asks for a job. After one conversation he is called established and trusted, two words that between them undo a decade, and his reply names a post rather than a reward. He then describes himself with two more words: a careful keeper, and knowing. Commentators note that he asks for the hardest office in a famine rather than for safety, and that his self-description is a statement of fitness rather than a boast.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, heard by a community with no access to power and little expectation of any. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators discuss whether Joseph's request amounts to seeking office, and generally read it as accepting a burden he was uniquely qualified for at the moment it was needed, since the plan was already his and nobody else in the country could carry it out.

keyTerms.gloss: I will keep him for myself
keyTerms.note: From the root meaning to make something pure and unmixed, the same root behind sincerity. The king wants him reserved exclusively, which is the language of possession dressed as honour.

A rhyming pair used only here in the Quran. The first word means firmly placed with real standing, the second means safe to rely on, and together they answer both charges Joseph had been living under.
The first word is the one his brothers had twice claimed for themselves when promising to look after someone. In their mouths it failed twice. Here it is finally used by a person who means it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Storehouses were the real seat of power in a grain economy. Whoever held the keys decided who ate during a famine, at what price, and on what terms, and such an office made a man wealthy or hated within a season. Arabian listeners knew the smaller version: the man who controlled a well during drought controlled everyone who needed it, and his character determined whether that was a mercy.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words the king uses of Joseph, established and trusted, occurs only here in the Quran, and so does the pair Joseph uses of himself. Two rhyming descriptions, both unique to this exchange, are set opposite each other across a single conversation, which is the sort of symmetry the surah repeatedly builds into its dialogue.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance on God is shown as compatible with competence and with asking for responsibility. Joseph does not wait to be given a role and does not pretend he lacks the skill for it, and the surah presents that as continuous with everything he has done. The passage also completes a long reversal quietly. The words for trustworthiness and safekeeping, which people in this story kept misusing, are finally attached to someone who has earned them.

crossReferences.why: The brothers first claim the word for safekeeping, in a promise they break within a day.
Jacob takes the same word away from people and gives it to God as the better keeper.
Another moment of hiring where strength and trustworthiness are named as the qualifications.

studies.applyIt: If you know you are good at something that is currently needed, say so plainly to the person who decides. Not as a pitch and not with apology. Name the thing and name why you can do it. Many people wait to be noticed for years in a room where one accurate sentence would have been enough.

studies.title: To Dwell Where He Wished
studies.meaning: The sentence is a repetition, and the repetition is the point. Thirty-five ayat earlier the same words described a boy bought for a household in Egypt. Here they describe a man free to settle anywhere in the country. Nothing in the wording has changed; only the scale has. What follows is a clause about mercy reaching whom God wills, and then a promise phrased negatively: no reward of those who do good is ever lost. The surah prefers that formulation to a guarantee of success.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and heard by people whose prospects were narrowing rather than widening. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators emphasise the timing rather than the elevation: Joseph is settled just before a famine that will bring his family across a desert to his door, so what looks like the end of one story turns out to be the arrangement for the next.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a firm position. The verb means to give someone a footing from which they can act, and the Quran uses it of nations as well as individuals, always as something granted rather than seized.
A verb for choosing where to settle and making a place your own. Said of a man who arrived in the country as merchandise and lived in a cell, it carries the whole reversal in one word.

The promise is negative rather than positive. It does not say the reward arrives soon or in a recognisable form, only that nothing spent in doing good is mislaid, which is a narrower and steadier claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Freedom of movement was the visible mark of status. A slave went where he was sent, a client went where his patron allowed, and only a man of standing chose his own town and travelled without permission. Arabian listeners measured position that way instinctively, by who could leave. The ayah spends one clause on Joseph's authority and one on his ability to go where he liked, and the second was the louder of the two.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about God establishing Joseph in the land appears twice in this surah, in identical wording, once when he is sold into a household and once when he takes charge of a country. The first time it is attached to being taught; the second time to living wherever he wishes. The same sentence covers a slave's arrival and a minister's freedom.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is described as reaching whomever God wills, and in the same breath as never wasting what good people do. Held together, the two clauses keep grace from being either arbitrary or earned. The passage also gives the surah's answer to a reader's obvious question about the wasted years. Nothing was lost in them, and the establishment here is presented as the same act of God that put him in a stranger's house.

crossReferences.why: The first use of the identical clause, at the point where he is bought as property.
Restates the same promise in Joseph's own mouth, once he can see how it worked.
Repeats the negative form of the promise: We do not waste the reward of those who act well.

studies.applyIt: Think of an effort of yours that came to nothing visible: the job you did well before being let go, the kindness nobody registered. Rather than deciding it counted or did not, try holding it as filed somewhere you cannot see. That is the exact claim this ayah makes, and it asks for no feeling from you beyond leaving the question open.

studies.title: And Then His Brothers Came
studies.meaning: One ayah of comment and one of narrative, and the join is abrupt on purpose. The comment relativises everything just described: the reward of the hereafter is better, for those who believed and kept watch over themselves. Then, with no transition, the brothers walk in. He knew them and they did not know him. Commentators note the sentence's asymmetry, which is stated flatly and left there, since the whole of the next thirty ayat is contained in it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the famine that brings the brothers south fits what is known of periodic failures in the eastern Mediterranean grain supply. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators point out how much time the surah passes over here without narrating it, and note that the reunion is set up not by any plan of Joseph's but by hunger, which reaches Canaan on its own schedule.

keyTerms.gloss: and the reward of the hereafter
keyTerms.note: The word for reward is the ordinary one for a workman's wage. Placing it against everything Joseph has just been given is a comparison of payments, not a dismissal of what he received.

From a root about placing a shield between yourself and harm. The Quran's central word for godliness is at bottom a word for carefulness, and the imperfect tense here makes it a habit rather than an achievement.

The active participle of a verb meaning to fail to know something you should know. The same root gives the word for what is wrong or disowned, so failing to recognise carries a faint charge in Arabic.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Famine moved people along known roads. When Canaan's harvest failed, families sent their strongest men south with whatever they could trade, and Egypt's officials rationed grain by household to whoever appeared. Arabian audiences knew the pattern from their own droughts, when whole clans travelled towards water and towards relatives with stores. Nobody in that world regarded arriving at a stranger's door with a bag of goods as beneath them.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah passes over roughly twenty years between one ayah and the next, from Joseph's appointment to his brothers' arrival, without narrating a single event in them. The seven good years and the beginning of the famine happen in the white space between two sentences, which is how this surah handles time throughout: slowly at the turning points and not at all in between.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comment placed just before the reunion prevents a misreading of the whole story. Joseph's rise is not the payment; it is an episode, and the ayah says the real wage lies elsewhere and is better. That protects the surah from becoming a promise that patience produces power, which would be untrue and cruel to most of its readers. The narrative resumes only after the correction has been made.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same comparison at the surah's close, addressed to the listeners rather than to Joseph.
The moment the asymmetry ends: he names what they did while they still do not know him.
States the same preference plainly, that the home of the hereafter is better for the mindful.

studies.applyIt: Notice one good thing you have that you half expect to settle an account for you: a title, a house, being right about something. Say to yourself once today that it is an episode. Not that it is worthless, only that it is not the payment. The sentence takes three seconds and it loosens the grip a little.

studies.title: I Fill Up The Measure
studies.meaning: He loads their camels first and makes his request afterwards, which is the shape of the whole ayah. Then he offers evidence rather than authority: look at how I have dealt with you, I give full measure and I host well. Commentators note that the demand for the youngest brother is wrapped inside a demonstration of trustworthiness, and that the men he is speaking to have no way of hearing the request as anything but the reasonable condition of a generous official.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a trading city where short measure was the standard complaint against merchants and where a reputation for filling a container honestly was worth real money. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that Joseph is now administering rationing during a famine, an office where shorting people was easy, expected and almost impossible to prove.

keyTerms.gloss: I give the measure in full
keyTerms.note: The verb means to complete something so that nothing is owing. Measuring grain was done by volume into a vessel, and completing it meant filling to the brim rather than to the convenient line.

Literally the best of those who give lodging. Hospitality in that world was an obligation with a public standard, so the claim is measurable rather than boastful, and his guests had just experienced it.
The indefinite phrasing is careful. He does not say the youngest, or name him, or reveal that he knows anything about the family beyond what they have told him at the counter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grain was sold by the measure, poured into a standard vessel and levelled off, and the whole trade turned on how the levelling was done. Short measure was the classic dishonesty of markets from Mecca to Damascus, and the Quran addresses it more than once. A man who filled to the brim during a famine, when he could have named any terms he liked, was doing something everyone in the queue would notice.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for measure recurs through this half of the surah, in Joseph's mouth, in his brothers' request to their father, and in what they find in their baggage. A story about a family's reconciliation is conducted almost entirely in the vocabulary of the grain market: measures, loads, goods, saddlebags and the price of a camel's burden.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Generosity is presented as the thing that makes a hard condition bearable. Joseph attaches his demand to a record his hearers have just witnessed, and the surah lets that stand as the ordinary way trust is built between strangers. It also shows integrity in an office where nobody could have checked him. Filling the measure during a famine is exactly the case where honesty costs and cannot be verified.

crossReferences.why: The brothers return in worse straits and ask for the same full measure as a charity.
Describes giving full measure and a true balance as better and finer in the end.
Names the practice this ayah reverses: taking full measure from others while shorting them.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where you round in your own favour and nobody would notice. The last ten minutes of a shift, the change from a shared bill, the answer you give slightly shorter than it should be. Do that one thing to the brim today. The exercise is not about the amount. It is about doing it where no verification exists.

studies.title: We Will Work On Our Father
studies.meaning: The condition is stated twice over, once as a loss and once as an exclusion: no measure from me, and do not come near me. Then the brothers answer with a verb worth noticing. They say they will work on their father to get the boy released, using the same word the surah used for a long campaign of persuasion in an Egyptian house. Commentators observe that the brothers do not hesitate or object. Grain matters more to them than an old man's fear.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Food during a shortage was distributed by whoever held the stores, on terms nobody could negotiate, and being cut off from a supply meant a family's survival was at stake within weeks. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that Joseph's condition is severe and read it as a test rather than a threat, since the surah shows him afterwards arranging for the brothers to be able to return.

keyTerms.gloss: and do not come near me
keyTerms.note: A prohibition of approach rather than of trade, which raises the cost from commercial to personal. In a world where access to a powerful man was itself a kind of wealth, exclusion was the sharper half of the sentence.

The same verb used earlier in the surah for a long campaign of persuasion applied to Joseph himself. It means gradual, repeated pressure, and the brothers use it of their own father without any apparent discomfort.
An emphatic construction promising action. The surah has heard this register from them before, in the guarantees they gave about Joseph, and the repetition is not accidental.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trading parties travelled as family units and negotiated as one, and the men who went south for grain carried the household's whole hope with them. A condition attached to the next journey bound everyone at home to it, whether they had agreed or not. Listeners in Mecca understood the arithmetic instantly: a family that cannot return to the granary in a famine year has to decide what it will trade for access.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb the brothers use for persuading their father is the same one the surah used for the sustained approaches made to Joseph in the governor's house. It appears only in this surah and carries the idea of pressure applied repeatedly over time, so one word links a campaign against a young man's integrity with a campaign against an old man's fear.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows need doing what argument could not. The brothers have not changed and are not repenting; they are simply hungry, and the surah is candid that this is what moves them. Being honest about mixed motives is a consistent feature of Quranic narrative. People are brought where they need to be by ordinary pressures, and the story does not pretend the pressure was piety.

crossReferences.why: The campaign begins, and it uses the identical guarantee they gave about Joseph years earlier.
Jacob's answer, which finally extracts a pledge rather than a promise.
The earlier use of the same verb for persuasion, applied to Joseph behind closed doors.

studies.applyIt: Notice this week when you find yourself building a case to bring to someone. That is a normal thing to do and it is worth watching. Before you deliver it, ask one question: does this person have a reason for their position that I have not asked about. Then ask them, before the case.

studies.title: Put Their Goods Back
studies.meaning: The instruction is given to servants, not to the brothers, and that is what makes it work. Their payment goes back into their saddlebags where they will find it at home, so the gift arrives without a giver present to be thanked. The stated purpose is practical: perhaps they will recognise it and come back. Commentators read the act as generosity and strategy at once, and note that Joseph never mentions it afterwards, not even when the family is finally reunited.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and heard by a community for whom hospitality and quiet help between households were the daily fabric of survival. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators observe that Joseph is spending the state's grain and returning private payment, and that the surah records the transaction without comment, which they take as an indication that the arrangement was within his authority as keeper of the stores.

keyTerms.note: The same word used earlier for Joseph himself when he belonged to a household, and for his two companions in prison. Here it names the men who work for him, which quietly completes a reversal.

The packs strapped to a travelling animal. The word recurs at the surah's next turn, when a cup is placed in a saddlebag rather than money, so the same hiding place serves a kindness and then a stratagem.

The verb means to come back, and across the Quran it also carries the sense of turning back in repentance. Both readings sit comfortably here, since what Joseph wants is their return in more than one sense.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Saddlebags were opened at the end of a journey, in front of the family, and the unpacking was a small public event. Everyone gathered to see what had been bought and what had been kept. Slipping payment back into the packs meant the discovery would happen at home, among everyone, at the exact moment the case for a second journey needed to be made. It was a well-designed gift.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for saddlebags appears three times in this surah and each time something is concealed in them: first the returned payment, then the king's drinking cup, then the sentence the brothers pronounce on whoever's bag holds it. One ordinary piece of travelling equipment carries a kindness, a stratagem and a reckoning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Generosity here is deliberately hidden, and the passage neither praises the concealment nor explains it. What it shows is a gift arranged so that the receiver cannot be embarrassed by it, given by someone with every reason to want gratitude from these particular men. The surah's broader pattern holds: Joseph consistently declines the moments where he could have made himself the centre of the scene.

crossReferences.why: The discovery at home, and the effect it has on the family's argument about the journey.
The same saddlebags used again, this time to hide something that will accuse rather than help.
Describes concealed giving as better for the one who gives than giving in the open.

studies.applyIt: Give something once this month in a way that cannot be traced back to you. Leave it, send it through someone, pay it forward without a name attached. Notice the small pull to be known for it, and let that pull go unanswered. That pull is the part of the exercise that is actually doing something.

studies.title: Send Our Brother With Us
studies.meaning: They report the difficulty accurately and then close with the same guarantee they gave about Joseph, in almost the same words: we will take care of him. Nothing in the surah suggests they hear the echo. Commentators note that they lead with the loss of the measure rather than with the request, which puts the family's hunger in front of the father's fear before the sentence about the boy arrives. The argument is well made and it is built from a promise already broken once.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. A household in a famine year had a small number of choices and most of them involved sending someone away. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators read the scene as the surah's method of showing how little the brothers have changed: they return to their father with the same rhetorical shape they used before, and the words come out unaltered because nothing underneath them has moved.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb that avoids naming who withheld it. They present the condition as something that happened rather than as a demand made by a person, which makes it harder for their father to argue with.
A tightly compressed form meaning to obtain a measured allowance for ourselves. Arabic can fold a whole transaction into one verb, and the word puts grain in the sentence immediately after the boy.
Word for word what they promised about Joseph before the journey to the well. The surah repeats the phrase without any narrator's comment and lets the reader hear it against the earlier one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Decisions like this were taken in front of everyone. A household in a tent or a courtyard had no private rooms, and a father weighing whether to send his youngest away was doing it with his other sons watching and his womenfolk within earshot. Pressure in that setting was not a conversation but a slow accumulation of people needing an answer, which is what the next ayat show.
studies.didYouKnow: The promise the brothers make here repeats, with the same emphatic particle and the same participle, the promise they made about Joseph decades earlier. The Quran gives the reader no reminder and adds no comment. The repetition is left entirely to memory, which is one way a text that was heard rather than read teaches its audience to listen.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a family in which nobody has apologised and everyone still has to eat. That is an unglamorous and accurate picture of how households actually carry old injuries, and the surah does not resolve it here. It also shows a truthful report used as an instrument. Everything they say about the granary is accurate, and the accuracy is what makes the sentence at the end effective.

crossReferences.why: The original version of this promise, made about Joseph in almost identical wording.
Jacob answers by naming the earlier occasion directly rather than by refusing outright.
What he finally accepts instead of a promise: a pledge given before God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you have made more than once to the same person. Not a broken promise, just a repeated one. Say it differently this time, or say something smaller that you will certainly do. Repeating an unchanged sentence to someone who remembers the last time asks them to do all the forgetting.

studies.title: God Is The Better Guardian
studies.meaning: He answers a question with a question, and the question is a memory. Shall I trust you with him as I trusted you with his brother before. There is no accusation in it and no refusal either; the sentence simply declines to pretend the first occasion did not happen. Then he moves the word they had used about themselves, guardian, off them and onto God, and closes with a name for God rather than a decision. Commentators read the ayah as consent given without illusion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and heard by people asked to keep relying on God while the human arrangements around them kept failing. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that Jacob does not withhold the boy in the end, and read this sentence as the point where he stops guarding the outcome himself, which is what makes his eventual agreement something other than a surrender to pressure.

keyTerms.note: Built on the root behind safety and faith. To trust a person with someone is to declare them a safe place, and the question asks whether that declaration is available a second time.
A comparative that takes the word his sons twice claimed for themselves and gives it to God. The transfer is the whole argument: guardianship is not withdrawn from the world, only relocated.

keyTerms.gloss: the Most Merciful of the merciful
keyTerms.note: A superlative measured against other mercy rather than in isolation. It concedes that people can be merciful and then places God's mercy above the whole class, which is why it is said at the point of letting go.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sending a son on a journey meant handing him to the desert, to bandits and to whoever his companions turned out to be. There was no way to check on him and no message until the party returned. Every parent in that audience had done it, and the phrase about a better guardian describes the only thing available to a person watching a caravan get smaller on the horizon.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Jacob uses for God as the Most Merciful of the merciful occurs four times in the Quran and two of those are in this surah: here, when he releases his youngest son, and later in the mouth of Joseph when he forgives his brothers. Father and son reach for the same words at their two hardest moments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Trust in God is shown as something a person does with open eyes rather than as a substitute for judgement. Jacob knows exactly what these men are capable of, says so, and still lets the boy go, because the alternative is to guard something he cannot guard. The passage also refuses to make reliance a guarantee of outcome. What he names at the end is God's mercy, not a promise about the journey.

crossReferences.why: Joseph closes the reckoning with the same name for God his father used when letting go.
The promise his sons made the first time, using the very word he now takes from them.
What he asks for before agreeing, which is a pledge made before God rather than to him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are holding tightly because you do not trust the people who would otherwise carry it. Name honestly why you do not trust them, without softening it. Then hand over one small piece of it anyway, and say a line to God about the part you cannot watch. Both halves belong to this ayah.

studies.title: What More Could We Want
studies.meaning: The bags are opened and the argument wins itself. Their money is inside, and the sentence that follows is a piece of pure salesmanship: what more do we want. Then four benefits in a row, provisioning the family, guarding the brother, an extra camel-load, and the whole thing dismissed as easy trade. Commentators note the ordering. The care of the boy is listed third, between the household's supplies and the additional ration, and nobody in the room appears to notice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a city where a camel-load was a real unit of account and where the difference one extra made to a family in a lean season was understood without explanation. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that the returned payment does exactly what Joseph intended: it turns the second journey from a risk their father must accept into an opportunity the household cannot refuse.

keyTerms.note: A rhetorical question that closes discussion rather than opening it. The verb means to seek or to want, and framing the request this way makes any remaining objection sound like ingratitude.

keyTerms.gloss: and we will provision our family
keyTerms.note: A specific verb for fetching food supplies for dependants. It names the errand's real purpose in one word, and it is the first of the four benefits they list.

The adjective means small, light or readily obtained, and commentators read it both ways: a modest amount not worth refusing, or a quantity easy to come by. Either reading makes the request sound trivial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rationing during a shortage was done per head, and one more man in the party meant one more camel-load of grain. For a large household that was the difference between eating through a season and running out before it ended. The arithmetic was public and everybody could do it, which is why the brothers can make their case in a single sentence and expect it to land.
studies.didYouKnow: Their list of reasons puts the youngest brother's safety third of four, after supplies for the household and before an extra camel-load of grain. The surah reports the sequence without comment and never returns to it, leaving the ordering to do its own work on a listener who has been following this family since its first council.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows how an unexpected gift becomes an argument. Nothing they say is false, and the whole speech is shaped by the relief of finding money they thought they had spent. The Quran is often exact about this: sudden ease loosens judgement, and a good turn received can be the very thing that carries people into a decision they had been resisting for sound reasons.

crossReferences.why: The instruction that put the money there, and the effect it was designed to have.
Their father's answer, which refuses the arithmetic and asks for something binding instead.
Names wealth and children as a trial, which is precisely the pressure operating in this room.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the sentence what more could we want in your own mouth this week. It usually arrives just after something unexpectedly good and just before a decision. When you hear it, name the thing that is actually being risked, out loud, once. Then decide. Often the decision is the same and it is now yours.

studies.title: A Pledge Before God
studies.meaning: He stops accepting promises and asks for something else: a binding undertaking taken in God's name, with one exception written into it. Unless you are overwhelmed. That clause is the interesting part, since it concedes in advance that circumstances can defeat honest men, and so keeps the pledge from being a guarantee nobody could keep. When they give it, he does not thank them. He says God is witness over what we say, which puts the agreement somewhere neither party can quietly revise.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Oaths sworn in God's name were the strongest instrument that society had, stronger than any writing, and breaking one destroyed a man's standing permanently. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators read Jacob's insistence as the natural response of someone whose sons' informal assurances had already failed once, and note that he asks for the pledge only after stating his condition plainly.

keyTerms.note: From the root for tying firmly, the same root behind the words for a rope and for a covenant. It names an obligation with a knot in it, not an intention, which is what he had been given before.
A passive verb meaning to be encircled with no way out. The exception covers being overpowered by events rather than changing your mind, and it is written into the pledge by the person demanding it.
The one to whom a matter is committed for keeping. Naming God as witness over the words themselves places the pledge beyond the reach of both parties, including the father who asked for it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Contracts in that world were spoken and witnessed. Two men clasped hands in front of others, invoked God, and the transaction held because everyone present would remember and repeat it. Writing existed but was rare and mostly commercial. The one thing stronger than a written record was a public oath, and the one thing that ended a man socially was being known to have broken one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the binding pledge in this ayah occurs three times in the Quran and all three are in this surah: twice here as Jacob takes it, and once later when the eldest brother recalls it in Egypt and refuses to leave. A single term carries the obligation from the moment it is given to the moment it is honoured.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Trust between people is shown needing a third party, and the surah puts God in that place rather than any human authority. The exception clause matters just as much. An undertaking that admitted no limits would either be broken or would force the brothers into an impossible position, and building the limit into the oath is what makes it honest. Realism about human capacity is treated here as part of good faith.

crossReferences.why: The eldest brother remembers this pledge in Egypt and refuses to leave because of it.
