The informal promise this replaces, which repeated a form of words already broken once.
Addresses covenants made in God's name and the weight carried by making Him the guarantor.

studies.applyIt: When you next agree to something that matters, build the exception in out loud. Say what would actually stop you, in one clause, at the moment of agreeing. It feels like weakening the promise and it does the opposite. Everyone knows the exception exists; naming it is what makes the rest of the sentence believable.

studies.title: Enter By Different Gates
studies.meaning: A practical instruction is given and then immediately stripped of any power. Do not go in as one group; enter separately. Then, in the same breath: I cannot protect you from God in anything. Commentators generally read the advice as a precaution against attracting notice, and note that Jacob takes the trouble to say his own precaution guarantees nothing. The ayah ends by moving from what he does to what he relies on, and then widens from himself to everyone who relies.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. A group of eleven brothers arriving together at a foreign city's gate would have been conspicuous, and travelling parties routinely split to avoid attention, tolls or trouble. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Some commentators mention the evil eye and others simple prudence about drawing notice; the surah names neither, and the classical discussions record the range without settling it.

keyTerms.note: The adjective is the one Joseph used in prison of scattered lords. Here dispersal is prudent and there it was the objection, so the same word carries opposite value in two mouths.
A verb for warding off need or harm. Jacob uses it of himself, which is unusual advice to attach to your own instructions, and it is the reason the ayah is not simply about tactics.
From the root for appointing an agent to act on your behalf. Reliance in this vocabulary is a delegation rather than a mood, which is why it sits so comfortably next to giving practical instructions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: City gates were where authority met travellers. Tolls were levied, strangers were questioned, and a large armed-looking party from outside the country attracted exactly the interest nobody wanted. Caravans commonly broke up before arrival and reassembled inside. The instruction would have sounded to the first hearers like ordinary road sense from a man who had been sending sons on journeys all his life.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about judgement belonging to God alone that Jacob uses here also appears earlier in this surah, spoken by Joseph in an Egyptian prison. Neither of them knows the other is alive. The Quran gives father and son the same formula, in the same surah, in circumstances as different as a cell and a departure at home.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance on God is defined here by what it does not replace. Jacob gives sensible instructions and then denies that his instructions can protect anyone, and both halves are presented as belonging together. The passage rules out two errors at once: the assumption that precaution is unbelief, and the assumption that precaution is what keeps you safe. The last clause turns the whole thing into a general rule for anyone who relies.

crossReferences.why: Joseph uses the identical sentence about judgement, years earlier and in a prison.
The narration's verdict on this advice: it availed them nothing, but it settled something in him.
Messengers under threat give the same closing formula about where the reliant should rely.

studies.applyIt: Do the sensible thing this week and say the other half out loud. Lock the door, then say plainly that the lock is not what keeps the house. Send the application, then say the same about the application. Most people do one or the other. Doing both in one motion is the shape this ayah is describing.

studies.title: A Need In Jacob's Soul
studies.meaning: The verdict on the previous instruction is blunt: it availed them nothing against God. Then the ayah says what it did accomplish, and the phrase is unusually tender. It was a need in Jacob's soul, which he settled. Commentators read this as neither praise nor criticism but description: a father did what he could, the doing changed no outcome, and it answered something in him. The closing clause then says he had knowledge because God taught him, and that most people do not know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's first hearers were people making small arrangements against very large pressures, and this ayah addresses that condition directly. No occasion is reported for it. The commentators note the unusual move of the narration passing judgement on a prophet's advice while immediately affirming his knowledge, which they read as separating the limits of a precaution from the standing of the person taking it.

keyTerms.note: The word covers a want, an errand and an unmet requirement at once. Applied to an inner state it names something a person has to discharge before they can rest, whether or not it changes anything outside.
The verb for completing something owed, used of debts and of decrees. It says the need was not merely felt but paid off, which is why the sentence reads as sympathetic rather than dismissive.

The same verb used at the surah's opening for what God would teach Joseph. Knowledge in this story is consistently traced back to a teacher, in both generations, and never treated as native shrewdness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in that world knew the small rituals that people perform when someone leaves: the words said at a departure, the way a bag is packed, the last instruction called after a rider. None of them keep anyone safe on a desert road, and everyone does them anyway. The ayah names that human behaviour precisely and does not mock it, which is why the sentence has stayed memorable.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places in the Quran where the narration comments directly on the effectiveness of a prophet's own advice, saying plainly that it changed nothing while affirming in the same ayah that he had knowledge from God. The two statements are placed side by side without any attempt to reconcile them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowing a great deal is compatible with acting on a limited plan, and the passage refuses to make that a contradiction. Jacob's knowledge is real, God-given, and does not extend to controlling what happens at a foreign city gate. The ayah also grants dignity to the human need that produces such precautions. Doing what you can is treated as something a person owes themselves, quite apart from whether it works.

crossReferences.why: The instruction this ayah judges, along with Jacob's own disclaimer about its power.
Jacob says again that he knows from God what his sons do not know.
Returns to the same theme: above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small thing you do that cannot possibly affect the outcome, and that you would feel wrong skipping. Checking the door twice, a phrase you say when someone drives off. You do not need to defend it or stop it. This ayah says a need was settled, and leaves that as a real thing that happened.

studies.title: I Am Your Brother
studies.meaning: The disclosure is made to one person and kept from ten. He draws his brother to himself, says who he is, and adds a single instruction: do not grieve over what they used to do. Commentators note what is absent. There is no explanation, no plan shared, no request for secrecy stated in the text, and no promise about how this ends. What the younger brother is given is a fact and a permission to stop carrying something, which is all the scene contains.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and read by the earliest audience alongside their own experience of families divided by the new message, where some members knew things others could not be told. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators observe that the youngest brother has grown up in the household that lost Joseph, which is the situation the instruction about grief is addressed to.

keyTerms.note: A verb for taking someone into shelter, used of giving refuge as well as of an embrace. It occurs twice in this surah and both are reunions: this one, and later when his parents arrive in Egypt.
Three words with no title, no office and no account of the intervening years. The most powerful man in Egypt identifies himself by the one relation that has no rank attached to it.
A form of the verb for hardship and misery, meaning to be brought low by grief. The negation is gentle rather than commanding, closer to you need not than to you should not.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A younger brother in a large household grew up inside a story he had not witnessed. He would have heard about the missing son at every gathering, seen his father's grief become a fixed feature of the house, and known he was the surviving half of a pair. Everyone in that audience understood how a family's central loss shapes the childhood of whoever comes afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for drawing someone into shelter occurs twice in this surah and nowhere else in it. Both occurrences are reunions in the same room in Egypt: first when Joseph takes his brother to himself, and later, thirty ayat on, when he does the same for his parents. The word bookends the family's return.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates relief from resolution. Nothing about the brothers' guilt is settled here and nothing is forgiven; one person is simply released from grieving over it. That distinction runs through the surah, which repeatedly gives people what they need before it gives them what they are owed. It also shows a man with total power over his family choosing, for the moment, to use it on one person's sorrow.

crossReferences.why: The same verb of shelter used again, when his parents finally reach him in Egypt.
Where the disclosure is finally made to everyone, and the reckoning is opened and closed.
Their father, still in Canaan, sending them out with the same refusal to give up on grief.

studies.applyIt: There is someone carrying a family sadness that is not really theirs: a younger sibling, a child, someone who arrived after the difficult years. Tell them one true thing this week that they were not told at the time. Not the whole account. One fact, and permission to stop holding the part that was never theirs.

studies.title: Do Not Despair Of Relief
studies.meaning: An old man who has lost two sons sends the rest out to search, and the instruction has two halves that do not obviously belong together: go and look, and do not despair. The commentators note the pairing, since searching is what a person does who has not given up. The word rendered as comfort is the one for a breath of relief. The sentence then defines despair by who does it, which is the sharpest thing in the ayah.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah revealed during a difficult stretch when little was going well for the community. Jacob has by this point lost Joseph decades earlier and Benjamin recently, and has been told his sons were involved in both. The commentators read his instruction as the surah's centre of gravity, since everything after it moves quickly towards a reunion nobody in the story expects.

keyTerms.note: A verb built from the root for sense perception, meaning to feel your way towards information. It describes patient, active searching rather than a formal inquiry, which is why it suits a decades-old loss.
From the root that gives the words for wind and for spirit. It names relief as something arriving like moving air, and the commentators explain it as the mercy that brings ease after constriction.
The verb for abandoning expectation entirely. Its appearance twice in one ayah, first as a prohibition and then as a description, turns the second occurrence into the reason for the first.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: People disappeared. Caravans were raided, travellers died on unmarked routes, and a family might wait years for news that never came, with no authority to ask and no record to consult. Searching meant sending men to ask at wells and markets and hoping a description was recognised. Jacob's instruction describes the only method available, and everyone listening knew how rarely it worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for God's relief is written the same as the word for spirit and is closely related to the word for wind, and classical commentators discuss the connection. Reciters distinguish them by a vowel alone, so a listener hearing this ayah hears a word for breath being used of divine mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Despair is classified rather than merely discouraged, and that changes its weight: it is described as something believers do not do, so hopelessness becomes a statement about what a person takes God to be like rather than a passing mood. The ayah also refuses to separate hope from action. The same sentence sends people out to search, so trust is what keeps a search going rather than a substitute for it.

crossReferences.why: Forbids despair of God's mercy in the widest terms, addressed to everyone.
Has Abraham ask who despairs of his Lord's mercy except those who are astray.
Shows the relief arriving, carried by the shirt he had been waiting for.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you stopped hoping for and quietly stopped working on at the same time. Do one small piece of the work again this week: send the message, make the enquiry. The ayah puts searching and hope in a single sentence, and the searching is the part you can actually start today.

studies.title: No Blame On You Today
studies.meaning: The brothers make a full admission with no excuse attached, and the reply is shorter than the confession. Joseph removes the charge, using a word for reproach that keeps being brought up rather than for a verdict passed. The commentators discuss the word for today, which some read as marking a limit and others as emphasis. He then hands the forgiving of the sin itself over to God rather than granting it, and closes with the widest name for mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah addresses a man whose own tribe had driven him out and who would one day be in a position to answer them. Classical sources record that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) used words close to these at the conquest of Mecca, and the commentators note the connection, though the surah had come many years before that event.

keyTerms.note: A word for blame repeatedly brought up again, from a root connected with reproving. What is removed is not the fact of the wrong but the continued raising of it, which is a precise thing to renounce.
From a root for a trace or a mark left behind. The brothers use it to admit the favour they had resented, so their confession names the exact thing that set the whole story moving.
A superlative set against the plural of the same word, so mercy is compared to mercy rather than to anything else. It ends the scene by pointing past the man who was wronged.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reconciliation in tribal society was formal and expensive. A wrong was settled by payment, by public acknowledgement before witnesses, and often by a marriage that tied the parties together afterwards. Simply cancelling a claim was rare, because it left the injured party without standing. Joseph holds complete power over men who had sold him, and the audience would have expected terms.
studies.didYouKnow: The brothers' confession and Joseph's reply together take fewer words in Arabic than the account of the crime they are discussing. Classical commentators note the brevity, and observe that the reply contains no reference to what was actually done, no conditions attached, and no request for anything in return.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is separated into two acts and only one of them is claimed. Joseph cancels the reproach that was his to cancel, and refers the forgiving of the sin to God, which keeps the wronged party from occupying a position he does not hold. The scene also shows pardon issued from strength rather than from necessity, which is the only condition under which it means very much.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether those with means would not rather have God forgive them in turn.
States that pardon and reconciliation carry a reward with God.
Shows the father promising to seek forgiveness for them, completing the scene.

studies.applyIt: Think of an apology you accepted while quietly keeping the incident available for later use. Decide today whether you will actually stop bringing it up. That is the specific thing the word in this ayah renounces, and it is a decision rather than a feeling, which makes it possible on a day you do not feel generous.

studies.title: Receive Me In Submission
studies.meaning: The prayer opens by listing what was given, authority and the reading of events, and both are named with a word meaning some of, not all. Then a divine title about originating the heavens and the earth, which widens the frame at exactly the point of triumph. The two requests are unexpected from a man at the height of his power: to die in submission, and to be joined to the righteous. Nothing at all is asked for in this life.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the close of the surah's narrative, after the family is reunited and the dream from the fourth ayah is fulfilled. The commentators note that the story ends not with the reunion but with a prayer, and that the Quran gives Joseph the last words of his own account. The surah then turns directly to the Prophet's own situation in its final ayat.

keyTerms.note: The preposition means part of. He describes what he was given as a portion rather than as dominion, which the commentators read as deliberate modesty at the moment he could have claimed most.
From a root for splitting something to bring it into being, used of a seed breaking open or of a first opening. It names creation as an initial rupture rather than as assembly from parts.
A verb for taking something in full, used of collecting a debt paid completely. Death is described as a receiving of what is owed rather than as an ending or as a loss suffered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Egypt was the granary of the region, and its administration was the most sophisticated bureaucracy the Arabian audience knew of by reputation. A man holding the stores during a famine held everything. Meccan traders bought Egyptian grain and cloth, and the scale of that state was proverbial. This prayer is spoken by someone at the top of the one system everybody agreed was formidable.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the very few places in the Quran where a prophet asks to die in a particular state, and the request comes at the point of his greatest worldly success rather than in difficulty. Classical commentators discuss the timing, and note that what is asked for is company as much as an ending.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer reads the whole story backwards and finds a giver behind every stage of it, including the parts that looked like ruin at the time. Naming God as protector in this life and the next collapses the two into a single relationship. And the requests locate the real object: not the sovereignty just described, which he treats as a portion already received, but a manner of dying and a company to join.

crossReferences.why: Promises him the same teaching of interpretation at the very start of the story.
